newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says Cuba compromise only a first step.
newsitem.headline: Canada says Cuba compromise only a first step.

text.p: Canada said on Friday that a U.S.-European Union deal to settle their dispute over Washington's anti-Cuba legislation was a good first step but did not resolve Canadian objections to the Helms-Burton law.

"It's the best breakthrough we've had," Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton told reporters, but he added that further negotiation with the United States through the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development was needed before Canada would be satisfied.
"I want to get rid of Helms-Burton," he said. "I want them to either amend it or end it."
He added that if the United States persisted with the legislation, he would challenge it under the North American Free Trade Agreement.
"I still have that in my back pocket," he said. "I will use it if it's necessary."
He said the agreement with the EU did not change anything for the Europeans nor for the companies that have been blacklisted by the United States.
The European Commission said on Friday that it struck a deal with the United States over the controversial Helms-Burton law, which punishes foreign firms for doing business with Cuba.

The United States and Canada have been at odds over the measure. Executives of Canadian miner Sherritt International Corp. have been banned from entering the United States under the law because of the company's operations on the communist-ruled island.
The EU and the United States reached an agreement just days before the EU presented its complaint at the WTO.
EU Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan said in a statement that the deal would "chart a path toward a longer-term solution through amendment to the Helms-Burton Act."

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien discussed the Cuba dispute with U.S. President Bill Clinton on a visit to Washington. The two leaders agreed to disagree on the best way to encourage democracy in Cuba.

While Canada maintains that its commercial and diplomatic ties to Cuba will encourage the Castro regime to improve democracy and human rights, the United States argues that its embargo of Cuba is the best approach.
Eggleton said the OECD will provide a better forum to negotiate changes to the Helms-Burton law than the World Trade Organisation, since the OECD will allow for a broader discussion.
